title: Testing fictional worlds
text: Briggs tested games alongside their writers-programmers. Testing included finding plausible player actions that a fictional world had not accounted for, not just crashes or coding errors.
brief: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.

title: Choosing romance
text: Romance was her own choice, not management's assignment. She wanted an adventure written from a female perspective and disliked the trivial cooking or sewing games then sold to girls.
brief: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.

title: Players and the heroine
text: Some reviewers disliked the heroine's permitted actions and wanted a stronger fighter. Briggs regarded romance as a legitimate form, even when critics treated a woman writing for women as a limitation.
brief: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.

title: Becoming an author
text: Steve Meretzky encouraged her to apply as an implementer. Her application game used an abstract setting so realistic details would not expose gaps in her implementation skills.
brief: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.

title: Working conditions
text: Infocom initially allowed writers considerable freedom. Briggs later remembered creative neglect and trust fondly; after Cornerstone failed and Activision acquired the company, layoffs and micromanagement changed her experience.
brief: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.

title: Editing and bugs
text: She spent months cutting a completed Plundered Hearts to fit machines including the Commodore 64. She linked frequent player deaths to simplifying puzzles and remembered bugs that escaped testing.
brief: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.

title: Sales and next projects
text: Management wanted another commercial hit, while her vampire and Doctor Who proposals went nowhere. Plundered Hearts sold about half Infocom's average; she eventually left amid demands without clear creative direction.
brief: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.

title: Readers and the medium
text: Years later, players told her the game had mattered to them, despite its disappointing sales. She understood text adventures as closer to books than films, involving imagined environments and play.
brief: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
